translations.text: The third against the pagans.
On the third day in Tripoli, Peter rose early from sleep and went into the garden,
where abundant water flowed continually. After bathing there, he prayed and sat down. As we sat around him, he noticed that we were looking at him, expecting to hear something.

He said, “I think there is a great difference between those who do not know and those who are mistaken. For I think someone who does not know is like someone who does not wish to go to a prosperous city,

because he knows nothing of the good things there. But someone who is mistaken is like someone who has learned about the good things in that city, but, while traveling toward it, takes a different path and so loses his way.

“Likewise, I think there is a great difference between these people. Those who worship idols do not know about eternal life, and so they do not desire it either. For a person cannot love something of which he has no knowledge.
But those who have chosen to worship the one God and have learned that eternal life is given to the good, if afterward they either believe or

do anything contrary to what pleases God, are like people who left a city of suffering to go to a prosperous city, but strayed from the straight road as they traveled.” While he was saying these things to us,
one of our companions came in and announced, “My lord, large crowds are standing at the gate.” When he gave permission, a great many people came in. He,
however, stood in the same place as yesterday, greeted them according to the custom of godliness, and said, “God is the one who created heaven and earth and made everything in them.
As the true Prophet told us, the human being was made in his image and likeness and was appointed to be lord and ruler over everything.
I mean the things in the air, on the earth, and in the water, as we can see from the facts themselves: through his intelligence he brings down the creatures in the air and brings those in the depths
upward. He hunts the creatures on the earth, although they are much greater in strength than he is—I mean elephants, lions, and other creatures like them. Thus, while he was righteous,
he was also above all suffering, and, since his body was immortal, he could not feel pain. But when he sinned, as we explained yesterday and before that,
because he became a slave to sin, he fell subject to every kind of suffering and was deprived of all good things by a just judgment.
For it was not right that, when the giver had been abandoned, his gifts should remain with the wrongdoers. But out of his great mercy, so that you might enjoy, along with the former good things,
the eternal good things to come as well, he sent his Prophet, and the Prophet sent us to tell you what you should think and do [?]. But the choice lies within your power.
These are the thoughts you ought to hold: that a person should worship God, the Maker of all. He is the one you are to receive into your minds. From him, along with
the former good things, you will also receive the eternal good things to come. You can therefore obey the things that help you if, to the evil serpent that has crept

into your minds, you say like enchanters, ‘You shall fear the Lord your God and serve him alone.’ Above all, then, this thought is helpful: that a person should fear him alone, not as someone unjust, but as someone just.
For a person fears someone unjust lest he be put to death unjustly, but fears someone just lest he be found guilty and punished.
Thus, through the single fear of him, you can be freed from many harmful fears. For unless you fear the one Lord and Maker of all, slaves to every evil, to your own harm,
you are—I mean slaves to demons, to passions, and to everything that can cause harm in any way. Take courage, then, and draw near to God, you who from the beginning were made to be lords

and to rule over everything. In your bodies you are his image, and in your minds you had the likeness of his thought. But because you did things belonging to the lot of animals without reason, your human soul
you have lost, and like pigs you have become dwelling places for demons. If, then, you accept God's law, you become human beings. For it was not to animals

Sorceries. It is said, “Do not murder,” and “Do not commit adultery,” and the rest of the other commandments. Therefore, do not begrudge yourselves the opportunity when you are called to return to your original freedom.
For it is possible, if through good deeds you become like God and are counted as his children because of your likeness to him, for you to become masters of everything.

Begin, then, to cast off the material objects of worship, the worthless idols, so that you may also escape slavery to injustice. For these have become your masters, although they are not even fit to be your slaves—
fit for your use. I mean the material of carved images, which have no life in them. These are not even fit to serve you, for they neither hear nor see,
nor do they smell or feel. They cannot even rest. Does any of you perhaps want to see as these things see,
or to hear as they hear, or to feel and move as they do? But far be it from me to insult with such an insult any human being who bears God's image,
even if they have lost the likeness in their understanding. So turn your gods, whether made of gold, silver, or some other material, back to your original use. I mean cups
and basins and the other things that are useful for serving you, so that the good things given to you from the beginning may once again be restored to you. But perhaps you will say, “The laws
of those who rule over us will not allow us to do this.” It is just as well that the power belongs to the law and not to these worthless objects of worship, which have none.
How could you suppose that they are gods, when they are subject to human laws, guarded by dogs, and carefully placed under lock and key? This is if they are made of gold, silver, or bronze. Those
made of stone or clay, materials of little value, are not guarded, because no one desires to steal a god of stone or clay. Those made of costly material, then, are in great danger.
How can they be gods when they are stolen, melted down, weighed, and guarded? Oh, the minds of wretched human beings, who, before something deader than the dead,
tremble! For I cannot even call these things dead, since they never even had power [?]. Are they not the tombs of people from long ago? For how often,
when someone is received in a foreign country, does he not recognize the shrines he sees, not knowing whether they are the tombs of dead human beings or of those called gods? But when

he asks and learns that they belong to gods, he worships and does not reject them. For if he had not asked and learned, he would have passed them by as tombs of the dead because of their similarity in appearance.
But I do not need to bring forward many proofs about this error. For anyone who wishes can easily understand that they are nothing,
unless perhaps someone fails to see what he sees. Therefore someone ought to stand before the worshiper and say, “You have become blind through what you worship.

You do not recognize that it does not see. But even now, hear that it does not hear, and understand that it does not understand. For these are hands made by the hands of a man who has died. Now, if the very person who made it has died,
how will something made by him not fall apart? Why, then, do you worship the work of a mortal, something that has no feeling at all? Those who have understanding do not even worship animals, nor

do they cause confusion over the elements that God made. I mean the heavens, the sun, the moon, the earth, the seas, and everything in them. For they have rightly concluded that they should not worship even the things from which

they were made, but should revere God, the Creator and giver of everything. For these created things themselves rejoice when no one offers them the honor belonging to the one who created them. For his alone is
the glorious praise belonging to the one who alone did not come into being, because everything else was made. Therefore, just as it is fitting that the one who was not made should be God,
so everything that came into being is not truly God. Above all, then, you must consider the crafty deception of the evil serpent who is among you, who cunningly leads astray

to you, and how he puts into your minds something advantageous [?] within you, from the brain down to the smallest members you have. He considers your deception a great gain, for he is assured by the law established from the beginning
that if, by suggesting those who are called gods, he binds you so that you sin against the grace of that sole sovereignty alone, he will have a great reward through your downfall,

according to this reasoning: because dust was assigned as food to the one who was cast down to the earth because of sin, he is again allowed to eat, while your souls are thrown into the belly of the fire.

To make you suffer these things, he stirs up every kind of thought within you to your harm. For it is from him that all the evil, misleading suggestions concerning sole sovereignty are sown in your minds. The first is that you should not listen to the word of God

or drive away from yourselves ignorance, the cause of all evils. In this way he keeps you from knowledge. Then again, he persuades you that you have reasoned correctly in thinking that if someone does not hear the word of God, he is not liable to judgment.
Because of this, some people go astray and refuse to listen, so that they will not know. They do not understand that ignorance itself is enough to be a poison
that brings death. For if someone unknowingly takes a deadly poison, that does not keep him from dying. In the same way, sins by their very nature kill the person who sins,

even if he unknowingly does something he should not do. If, then, judgment comes upon those who do not hear the word, all the more will he punish those who refused to accept the fear of God. For anyone who refuses to learn, supposedly

so that he will not be condemned, is judged as someone who knows. For he knows what he refuses to hear. No trick, then, provides an escape before God, who knows what is in people’s hearts. Therefore flee from the cunning thought of the evil serpent,
which creeps about in your minds. For even if someone departs this world in complete ignorance of God,

he will receive condemnation because, although he lived in it for a very long time, he did not recognize its Creator or who was the good giver of the nourishment given to him. Therefore, as someone without understanding,
and as an ungrateful person and a contemptible servant, he will be rejected from the kingdom of God.

Again, that evil serpent creeps about within you, suggesting that you should think and say what perhaps many of you have already said: “We too know that there is one God, the Lord of all. But these too

are gods. For just as there is only one Caesar, but he has administrators, governors, prefects, commanders of thousands, and centurions under his authority, so likewise, although there is one great God,
who is like Caesar, these too are gods, like rulers subject to him: they obey him and administer our affairs.” Listen, then,
you into whom this thought has been poured by him as though from poisonous bile. I mean the evil suggestion conveyed by this analogy, so that in this way

you may understand good and evil. But you have not examined the matter; you do not even consider what you yourselves say. You put God in the place of Caesar, and those who are called gods in the place of those who are called rulers.
Yet you do not even remain consistent with your own analogy. For if you did, you would have to recognize that, just as no one is allowed to give the name of Caesar to someone else—

I mean to a governor, a prefect, a commander of a thousand, or anyone else, because the person who gives it will not live, and the person who accepts it is also put to death—so, by your own analogy, it is not permissible to give this name of God to another.
For whoever is found either giving it or accepting it dies. If, then, an insult committed by one human being against another incurs judgment,
how much more will those who introduce other gods suffer eternal punishment! And this is just, since they dishonor God, because it is the name given to them to honor his sole
sovereignty. If you could, you would dishonor him in every way. For this word “God” is not his true name. Yet you have taken it as it is and dishonored it,
although it was given to you so that, by using it, it might be counted for you as the true name. But you have subjected it to every kind of dishonor. For even the rulers of the Egyptians

Those who boast in the empty loftiness of their words and profess to know the courses of the stars, because of the evil notion that has crept into them, have subjected him to every indignity, as though to their image-makers [?].
For some of them have committed themselves to worshiping the bull called Apis, others a goat, others a [?], and others a snake, but also a dove, an onion, and wind from the belly,

and the discharge of filth, and the bodily parts of animals that cannot speak, along with ten thousand other things that are utterly filthy and improper. When Peter said these things, the people standing around him laughed.
In response to their laughter, Peter said, “You laugh at these things without realizing that you are even more ridiculous than they are. Rather, you are laughing at one another.
For through your own evil customs you have been buried in error, and you do not examine them. I too acknowledge that you were right to laugh at the Egyptians, because animals that cannot speak
are worshiped by people who can speak, even though these animals die. But listen to how they, in turn, laugh at you and say, ‘Even if we worship things that die,
still, they have power for a time. You, however, worship things that have never lived.’ Along with this they also say,
‘We want to honor the likeness of the one God, and because we have not discovered which likeness it is, we choose to honor all likenesses.’
But when they say these and similar things, they think their reasoning is more just than yours. Therefore you too should answer them, exposing their falsehood: ‘For it is not to honor the God

of truth that you worship these things. Otherwise, all of you would worship all likenesses. But this is how you actually behave: some of you consider an onion to be a god and fight against those who worship wind

from the belly. In this way, each of you honors some particular thing, and you mock one another’s objects of worship. Some, as though possessing a superior understanding, worship individual parts of animals,
one this part and another a different one.’ Yet how many of them remain puffed up to this day with that destructive notion!

And because they are ashamed of the filthiness that is plain to everyone, they want to draw these things into [?], and by other devices they want to uphold their murderous error. Yet we could also address their [?],

if we were near those over whom this whole painful disease of foolishness has gained control, bringing their souls into grave sickness. For it is not necessary to apply [?] to a healthy part of the body,

but only to one suffering from disease. Since, by laughing at the Egyptians’ practices, you have shown that you do not suffer from their disease, it was right for me to offer treatment for what you do suffer from—the disease lodged in you.
Whoever, then, [?] to worship God, to bring [?] to the disease lodged in you. Whoever, then, wants to worship God must first know what belongs to God’s nature alone,
something that cannot belong to another, so that, by contemplating it in him and not finding it in another, we may never mistakenly suppose that anything else is God.

Now what belongs to God’s nature alone is his superiority to everything, as the maker of everything. The maker is superior in power to what is made, just as the unlimited is superior to the limited. In appearance,
beauty belongs to him; in his inner being, blessedness; in understanding, perfection. Likewise, in other respects his superiority is beyond comparison. Since, then, to God alone

belongs, as I said, superiority to everything, and since the world and everything in it were made by him, one must say that nothing made by him can be compared with him. And if anything is not his equal, it cannot be God.
If, then, the whole world, however great it may be, cannot be God, a few parts of it cannot rightly be called gods. By ‘parts’ I mean the gods made by you from gold
and silver, bronze and stones, or other substances that constitute matter, created by mortal hands. But in reply to these arguments, let us see what, through a human mouth,
the evil serpent has breathed out. What do many of those who worship them say? ‘We do not worship gold or silver.’
“Nor do we worship wood or stones. For we too know,” they say, “that these are nothing but lifeless matter and the craftsmanship
of a mortal human being. Rather, it is the spirit dwelling in them that we call God.” Consider this statement, then. For because this visible thing

is easily proved to be nothing, they have taken refuge in something invisible, so that, since it is something unknown, they cannot be refuted. Yet those who say this also concede in their argument [?] that part of their carved images is not God,
but insensible matter. They are therefore obliged to show how they know that a divine spirit dwells in them. But can they show us that it is in them?
For it does not exist, and we do not believe those who claim to have seen it. Now, however, we will present proof that there is no spirit in them,
so that, when their very belief that a spirit dwells in them is refuted, those who love the truth may listen and abandon their insane thinking. But first of all, if it is because a spirit is
in them that you revere them, why do you also worship the tombs of certain people of old? Thus you are not consistent even in this. But if there were a spirit in them, they would, by themselves,
move about and speak. They would scatter the cobwebs woven over them. They would drive away those who plot against them and steal them, and kill those who take their ornaments.
But as things are, they do none of these things. Instead, they are like condemned prisoners—and especially those that are more valuable.
For they are guarded, as I have already said. For if the authorities did not demand levies and taxes from you on their account, because of the great profit
you receive through them— Or again, have they not often been plundered, broken up, and then divided among people? Or again, do not those who worship

them steal large quantities of their offerings, even more than outsiders do, because they despise their own objects of worship? “But what about their care?” they say. “How often have the thieves been caught!” This too is false.

For how many have not been caught! But if they say that some power exists in them because certain people have been apprehended, they are mistaken. For among those who violate tombs, too, some are caught,

while others remain undetected. Surely those who were caught were not apprehended through the power of the dead! The same must be understood about these gods that are stolen and searched for. But what do they say? “They have no concern at all for the carved images.”
Why, then, do you still take care of them and guard them, adorning, polishing, and washing them, performing [?], crowning them, and offering sacrifices? Understand from this that it is not

with sound judgment that you do this. For just as you burn offerings for the dead, so you also sacrifice and pour out offerings to your gods. Nor, then, is the illustration of Caesar and his officials adequate,
those whom you say administer our affairs, when you yourselves take care of them in every respect, as I said before. For they can do nothing. Otherwise, tell us what they administer or what
they accomplish, like the governors of the various regions. Or do they shine like the sun, these things for which you light lamps? Or can they bring down rain as the clouds do,
when they cannot even move themselves? Or do they produce fruit like the earth, these things to which you present sacrifices? Thus they can do nothing. And even if they could do something,
you would not be justified in calling them gods. For even the created elements should not be called gods, but only the one who established them, arranging absolutely everything for our use.
For it is God who has exalted humanity in every way. Because you are unaware of his goodness, you have honored the elements that he subjected to your service. But what
is there to say about the elements, when you have even made lifeless carved images, and not only worship them but also, like slaves, submit

to them in everything? Therefore you have sinned in what you have thought, and have enslaved yourselves to demons. But through the knowledge of God and through good deeds, you can even become masters.
and to command demons as slaves, and you will become children of God, heirs of the eternal kingdom.” When he had said these things, he commanded those who were afflicted by
demons and diseases to approach him. When they came before him, he laid his hands on them, prayed over them, and sent them away healed.
He reminded them and the rest of the people of this: “Remain here faithfully during the days when I am speaking here.”
When the crowds had left, Peter bathed in the water flowing there, together with those who wished to do so. He arranged for us to recline on the ground, and [?] thick branches of trees

for shade. We reclined comfortably, and then we ate. After he had blessed and thanked God for our satisfaction, according to the custom of the Hebrews, since there was still plenty of time, he gave us permission to ask him about

whatever we wished. There were twenty of us there, and he explained to each person whatever he asked. When evening overtook us, he entered the house where we were lodging, and we all lay down together with him.
The Fourth
On the fourth day in Tripoli, Peter rose early, found us awake, and greeted us. He went out to the place where water was flowing, to bathe and then pray.
We too went over in the same way. When we had prayed together and sat down, he immediately began to speak. But because daylight had arrived, he allowed the crowd to enter.
When a large number of people had entered, he greeted them as usual and then began to say: “Because of the great negligence you have practiced to your own harm,

your mind has produced [?] through many beliefs in harmful superstitions. You have become like land left uncultivated for lack of farmers, which needs a long time to be cleared, lest the true word given to you like good seed
be received by your mind and then choked by evil concerns, becoming barren of helpful deeds.

For this reason, those who care about their lives must constantly listen to the word, so that, in the short time remaining to them, they may strive with great diligence to cleanse away the evils accumulated over a long time.

For the end of each person’s life in the world is hidden from him. Strive to uproot the dense undergrowth from your hearts, and not little by little, for you cannot be cleansed that way: you have lain uncultivated for a very long time.

Moreover, even great diligence will not suffice to cleanse you unless you become indignant with yourselves and rebuke yourselves for the things in which you were entangled like contemptible slaves, obeying your evil desires.

In this way, pour out this righteous anger of yours upon your minds like fire upon uncultivated land. But if you do not have this fire of righteousness, learn what good things you have been kept from, to what punishment you have been consigned, and who it was that deceived you.
Then your mind will be awakened and, through the teaching of the one who sent us, will blaze with anger like fire,
and it will be able to burn up the undergrowth of desires. Believe me: when you are willing, you can accomplish everything, for you are the image of the invisible God.
For this reason, those who wish to fear God should not call an idol the image of God and say that it should therefore be feared. For the human being is the image of God.

Therefore, whoever wishes to fear God should honor the human being with righteousness, because the human being bears God’s image in the body. His likeness, however, is not [?] in everyone, but in the pure mind of a good soul.

Since we have learned that the human being was made in God’s image, we tell you to practice righteousness toward the human being, so that you may receive grace from God, who gave the likeness. Now the honor

due to God’s image, which is the human being, consists in providing food for someone’s hunger, drink for their thirst, clothing for their nakedness, care for their sickness, and shelter when they are a stranger;
and in visiting someone who is in prison and helping according to one’s means. Rather than mention everything one by one, I say this:
whatever good someone desires for himself [?], he should do for the person in need. Then a good reward will be credited to him, because he has practiced righteousness toward God’s image.

But if someone is unwilling to do these things, he will be punished as one who despises God’s image. How, then, can your claim be consistent, when you say that out of fear of God you honor every likeness
You worship, while in every way dishonoring his true image, which is the human being, through adultery, theft, murder, and all the other disgraceful acts. It was necessary
for you not to commit any of these evils through which a human being suffers distress. But now you commit all these things through which distress comes upon a human being.
For distress comes upon him [?] through killing [?] and theft, when something he possesses is taken away, and through all the other things that you do not want to happen to yourselves.
But because you listened to that crafty, evil [?] creeping creature and were led astray by dwelling on the worship of many gods, against the image,
the true image of God, you act unjustly. Yet you think you are practicing righteousness toward carved images that have no awareness.
But perhaps some people say in reply to these things, “If he had not wanted them to exist, they would not have existed, but would have been destroyed.” I too say this:
this very thing will happen when all human beings turn their minds toward him [?], and then this present world will be transformed.

But if you want him to act in this way, leaving nothing of all the things that are worshiped, tell us: which of all existing things have you not worshiped? Have not some of you worshiped the sun, some the moon, and others water?
And others worship the earth, others mountains, others plants, others seeds, and others a human being, as, briefly [?],
we have said. They worship these along with all the other things. God, therefore, would have had to spare none of these things,
nor even us, so that nothing would remain, either of the things worshiped or of those who worship them. This is truly the desire
of that evil serpent who has crept and crawled among you and has no pity on you. But far be it that this should happen!
For an unjust judgment may be administered by any human being, but not by God. It is not just for the same judgment to fall upon someone who does evil
and upon someone who suffers it, unless the one who is worshiped himself willingly accepts the honor that is owed to one alone. But what do they say? “Then it was necessary,” they say,

“for those worshipers to be killed by the God who exists, so that no one else would dare to do this.” But you are not wiser than he, you who say this, so as to give him instructions as though you were wiser than he.
He knows what he is doing. For he is patient with all those who are ignorant, being merciful
and like a father who sustains them, because he knows that righteous people are born even from the wicked. Moreover, even among those who worship these filthy things

that have no awareness, many have come to their senses, stopped worshiping them and sinning, taken refuge in God, and lived through prayers and good deeds. “But why,” they say, “should God not have prevented us altogether from thinking this thought?”
But when you say this, you do not understand what freedom is, or how goodness can truly exist [?]. Someone who is good by his own will is not truly good, because

he is not what he is by his own will. For this reason, freedom is the ability of every person actually to carry out good and evil deeds. Through these things God has made provision for a person to be a friend or an enemy [?].
“No,” they say, “rather, everything we think, he himself has made us think.” Stop! Why do you who say this blaspheme still further?
For if he himself stirs up every thought within you, he becomes the cause of adultery, murder, [?], and every blasphemy.
Stop dishonoring him, you who owe him praise and every honor. And do not say that God has no need of praise. Although he needs nothing, ought we not
with a sense of justice to repay, with the voice of praise, the good things we owe to him who has benefited us in every way?
But what do they say? “We do even more, since we also praise these things along with him.”
But when you say these things, you do not understand the deception that will come upon you. For just as, when many physicians promise to heal one sick person,
they cannot, while the one who can truly cure him does not offer his medicines, because he knows that while he heals [?], someone else receives the praise, so also God,
when he is sought together with others who have no power, does not help. “But why, then,” someone says, “does this offend God, if someone else receives the praise when he gives help?”
I say that even if it does not offend him, he does not wish to support error. But when he gives help, the idol that has done nothing useful is believed to be the helper.
The error is very great when the idol that has done nothing useful is believed in instead of God, who gives help. I too say that, were it not that great harm would come to
the person whose mind has yielded to those things that have no perception, God would tolerate even this. Therefore wake up for the sake of your lives, and consider what you ought to do.

For because God lacks nothing, he needs nothing and is not harmed by anything. Both the benefit and the harm are yours. In the same way, Caesar is not harmed when he is insulted, nor, when he is praised,

does he receive any benefit. Rather, the person who praises him is free from fear, while the person who insults him is in danger of death. Likewise, those who praise God, although they give him no benefit,
save their own lives in the same way. Those who insult him do him no harm either, but destroy themselves. “But why,” someone says, “is this conduct toward God not equal

to conduct toward human beings?” I too say that it is not equal. For the punishment of someone who commits an offense against something greater is great, while that of someone who sins against something lesser is smaller.

Therefore, just as God is greater than everything, so the person who offends against him will receive a greater judgment—not because God takes vengeance on him with his own hands, but because all created things are hostile over this
and by their nature hasten to repay him. For neither would the sun give its light to blasphemers, nor the earth its fruits,
nor the springs their water; nor is it possible for his soul to find rest in Sheol. Even today, before the end of the world,
while it still stands, all created things are hostile. For this reason the heavens do not give rain and dew in full, nor does the earth give its fruits. For this reason many perish from hardship.
Creation itself blazes with anger and turns toward vengeance. Whatever we enjoy now is because, in his kindness, he compels creation [?] to provide for us.

Thus all created things hasten to free themselves from you who insult the Creator of all. For even if you escape them by being released from the body, what will you do about your soul, which cannot perish?

For even the soul of the wicked is immortal, though it would have been better for them if it were not immortal. For when it is burned by the unquenchable fire under a sentence that never ends, and because it does not die from its suffering,
there can be no end to its torment. But perhaps someone will say, “You are frightening us, Peter.” Then teach us how we can speak in silence of things as they really are. For to speak otherwise
is impossible for us. If we remain silent, evils entangle you through ignorance; but if we speak, we are thought to be frightening you about something false. How, then,
can we charm the evil serpent that has crept into your minds and cunningly stirs within you thoughts hateful to God? Therefore, out of love for God, come to your senses, for this is for your benefit,
if you take refuge in him through good works. There is something in you that is hateful to God: foolish desire and a conceit of wisdom that confirms you in error.

Others say that God does not care about us. This is a lie. For if he truly did not care, he would not make his sun rise on the good and the evil, nor send his rain down on the righteous and the unrighteous.

Others say, “We are considered more righteous when we worship both him and carved images.” But I do not think that someone who distributes honor equally to the king, to dead bodies, and to discarded dung will escape safely.
But perhaps you will say, “You call the objects of our worship dung?” Yes, I say so, for you have made them useless by assigning them a place among objects of worship in your error.

Yet sometimes we make considerable use even of dung. But these things, as they now are, cannot even serve the purpose of dung, though they have been lavishly adorned and worshiped. How, then, can you say that you are righteous,
when you are more wicked than everyone? For this one incomparable sin, you are justly condemned to the destruction of your souls, if you persist in this way of thinking. For just as
we know that a son who directs to someone else, who is not his father, the honor he owes his father, who has done him many kindnesses, is disowned and excluded from the inheritance,
so, when he conducts himself according to his father’s wishes and repays his kindness, he rightfully becomes an heir.

Others say, “It would be a great wickedness for us to abandon what we received from our fathers. For this,” they say, “is equivalent to someone failing to safeguard a deposit entrusted to him.” Then again, according to this reasoning, even if a

person does evil, or practices impurity, he is not required to take thought for himself and choose better things, so that he does not act wickedly and go astray, but avoids doing wrong as his father did.
And again, how are those who say the following not foolish?

“Our whole reason for worshiping these things is to avoid troubling him”—as though God were troubled when he is honored and at rest when he is blasphemed by wrongdoers! Why, then, when rain is withheld,
do you continually look toward heaven and offer prayers and petitions? Yet once you receive what you asked for, you quickly forget. For when you have reaped
and gathered the fruit, you offer the firstfruits to those who are nothing, readily forgetting God, the giver. You eagerly assemble
in your [?] and your temples, and enjoy yourselves at your sacrifices. For this reason, some of you say, “We do these things merely for recreation and enjoyment.”
How cleverly, then, you have devised this statement, like foolish [?] upright judges of what was being said! For even if it were necessary
for someone to give himself over to pampering his body, where would it be more fitting to enjoy oneself: beside rivers and among trees, holding a feast in pleasant shade,

or where there is a reminder of the demons that dwell there in madness? For hands are cut off, others are pierced, and desire is aroused [?], along with madness, hair standing on end, and the tumult of those who are possessed,

and trembling and howling and all the other things deceitfully employed to astonish the simple, so that, when you see these things, you will offer your vows and offerings to those who are deader than the dead.

And why do you do these things gladly? Since the serpent lurking within you is unwilling to say, I will remind you that this is what is proclaimed to those who fear God: that they should be chaste and watchful,

that they should restrain their anger, that they should not take what belongs to others, and that they should live justly, peacefully, and properly; and that a person should endure the hardship of poverty when he has nothing, rather than fill himself

by taking what belongs to others. But among those called gods, the opposite of these things is practiced. Is there anything just in the things falsely commanded there? Even if you were keeping all the good commandments,
this one thing—that you did not know God—would be enough to bring a sentence of death against you. But when you gather in these places, which you gladly give over to them,
you get drunk and burn whole burnt offerings, so that the spreading smoke of your sacrifices draws even deaf and blind spirits by its smell to the place where they hold sway.
And so some of you become possessed, while others are filled with various desires,

and others are driven to defile themselves, and still others to murder and theft. For the abundance of blood poured out there, and the libation of wine, intoxicate the unclean spirits as well, and they creep into you [?]
and disturb you in dreams, and defile you with the many torments of lust. For through these so-called sacrifices you become filled with evil demons, who cunningly destroy you without

Recognize the deceit that has come upon you. For because of some distress, compulsion, desire, anger, or oppression, they drive you to hanging yourselves, to drowning, or to throwing yourselves down from a height, or to killing yourselves in madness.
They advise you to do this, or through one of the other passions they remove you from life. But they cannot cause any one of these things to happen to us.
Instead, they themselves are tormented by us whenever they inhabit someone, begging us to give them respite and to delay their departure from him. But perhaps someone will say:
“Even among those who fear God, many sometimes fall into these afflictions.” But I say that this cannot happen.
For the God-fearing person is the one I will describe: someone who truly fears God, and is not merely called by that name.
Someone who truly is such a person fulfills the commandments of the law given to him. But if someone acts wickedly, he is not righteous. For just as someone from among the nations, if he fulfills
the law, becomes a Jew, so, when he does not fulfill it, he is a pagan. For a Jew is someone who believes in God and keeps the law.

Through that faith he escapes the afflictions of desires, which resemble accusers. But someone who does not fulfill the law clearly departs from God's commandments because he does not believe in God. Therefore, it is not as a Jew,
but as a sinner that he is seized by the afflictions appointed from the beginning, justly, by God's will, to discipline sinners. Thus, then, to those who fear him,
afflictions are sent mercifully because of their lapses, so that through bodily suffering their sin may be exacted like a debt, with repentance,
and so that they may be raised up pure on the day of judgment. For all the [?] of this world deprive the wicked of eternal blessings.
Likewise, disciplinary punishments are sent upon Jews who transgress, to exact payment, so that they may pay here and be delivered from that eternal torment. For you cannot say such things
because you do not believe that the things to come exist as we describe them—that is, when everyone receives recompense.
For this reason, because you do not know what benefit there is in turning away from short-lived desires in order to receive eternal blessings,

you are held back. Therefore we wish to bring forward a demonstration to counter your blindness, so that, when you believe the promises made to those who fear God, you may be able, through good deeds, to inherit with us
that world in which there is no distress. But as we begin with statements that you do not accept, do not complain against us as though we were lying about the blessings that we wish for you too.

For we have not grudged you knowledge of the truth and the blessings that we have come to believe exist. Rather, we have pleaded for this very purpose: to make you fellow heirs with us of these blessings that we believe exist.
For this is how one must speak to those who do not believe. But we are beginning in truth. You cannot understand everything we say unless you first listen to the message as lovers of truth.

For even if now the serpent that has lurked within you stirs up countless evil thoughts [?] in your minds, and obstacles through which it wishes to trouble you, you must all the more resist it in this and continually
listen to us. For you must gather continually concerning the things about which you have been completely mistaken, so that you may learn how to drive it away. It cannot happen otherwise.
By “drive it away,” I mean that in your minds you should stand against its evil counsels.
And remember that from the very beginning, at the dawn of knowledge, it brought death upon the world. Therefore, when the true prophet found the world in great error,

and saw it surrendering to evil, he did not neglect peace toward them because they were living in error. For it is at the end that he brings wrath upon those who support evil. Likewise, through the knowledge that he set against error, and its flame in those who are awake, like fire—
that is, love toward the one troubling them—and through the word he gave, which resembles a sword, he killed error by knowledge. And thus he distinguished the living from the dead.
Thus, when evil was condemned by the knowledge of the truth, conflict was stirred up everywhere. For the sake of eternal life, a son was separated from his father to the utmost [?].
And a father from his child, and a mother from her daughter, and a daughter from the mother who bore her—in a word, relatives from their own families and friends from their companions.
But let no one say, “How is it just for children to be separated from their own people?” It is indeed very just.

For if, by remaining with them, they not only gave them no help but also did not perish with them, you would have been right to say this. But how is it unjust for someone who wants to live to separate from someone who does not want to live,
but instead wants to perish and to destroy others along with himself? Yet even so, those who knew the truth did not want to separate,

but to live with them and help with good teaching those who remained. But the stubborn, because they were unwilling to listen to them, themselves started hostilities and drove them away, persecuting them
with hatred. Yet while enduring these things, they had compassion on them as people hindered by lack of knowledge. And, instructed by wisdom, they prayed for those who were doing evil
to them, because they had learned that error was the cause of their wickedness. For their teacher himself, when he was crucified on the wood, asked his Father to forgive his killers their sin,
saying, “My Father, forgive them this sin, for they do not know what they are doing.” The disciples, then, were imitating their teacher when they prayed for
those who harmed them, as they had been taught. Likewise, even their own people hated them and drove them away. Yet they offered prayers even for those who were not their own people,
but were their enemies, and loved them as they had been commanded. But tell me, how did you love your own people? If it was because
you regard them as righteous, I agree with you. But if it was without discernment, I question you, for you can become their enemies over a trivial matter.
But if you love them with understanding, tell us who your own people are. Perhaps you will say, “The founders of our family lines.”

Why, then, did you not love him who is the origin of all, if you were doing this out of a sense of justice? But perhaps you say, “We have not seen him.” Was it for this reason, then, that, while you did not inquire about the giver of life,
you sought to please things that have no perception? But what if knowing who God is was difficult? You could have recognized who is not God and considered
that wood is not God, nor stone, nor bronze, nor anything else made from perishable matter. Were they not carved with iron? For the iron that carved them was softened by fire,
which itself is extinguished by water. Water, in turn, is moved by the wind, and the wind by God, the maker of everything. He, then, is the source.
For this is what Moses the prophet said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. The earth was hidden and unformed,
and darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God hovered over the waters.” For by the Word of God and by the Spirit [?], as though by hands, he created everything.

He separated light from darkness, and afterward stretched out these visible heavens, so that the upper region would be a dwelling for the angels of light, and this lower region would be for humanity, to be sustained by everything created for its sake.
For your sake, O human being, God commanded the waters to move away from the surface of the waters, so that land might appear to provide you with fruit. And he pierced openings in it,

so that springs might be given to you, and the [?] of the rivers might appear, and it might bring forth animals. In short, he spoke all these things into being so that everything might be prepared for you. Is it not for your sake that the winds blow to make the fruit grow,

and rain and dew come down, and the seasons of the year change? The sun and moon, together with the rest of the stars, rise and set for your sake, and the rivers and lakes, together with the other seas, [?] for you.

How, then, do you not realize that great honor has been given to you? Likewise, if you are ungrateful, great torment in fire is prepared for you, because you did not wish to know him whom, before everything else,

you ought to have known. Even now, then, advance from these little things and come to know him who is the cause of everything. Consider that everything came into being from water, while water, through the Spirit,
is stirred to bring forth life. The Spirit, in turn, is from God, who has authority over everything. By this line of thought you will be able to reach God.
When you recognize your lineage and are born anew from these waters that have existed from the beginning, you will become an heir of your own people, those who gave birth to you without labor pains.

Therefore approach readily, like a son approaching his father, so that God may attribute the cause of your sins to ignorance. But if, after being called—so that the cause of your sins may be attributed to ignorance
by God—but if, after you are called, you are unwilling or delay, you will perish by God's just judgment, because you were unwilling to accept those who desired you.

And why do you suppose that you alone, out of all who have existed since the beginning of the world, will be righteous? Yet without baptism you cannot receive hope. Or perhaps, indeed, you will instead endure great torment because you did not perform good deeds rightly.

It is good for someone to do what is good when it accords with what God has said. But if you are unwilling to be baptized in water as he has pleased, because you obey your own will, you become an enemy of what pleases him.
But perhaps someone will say, “How is a person helped toward righteousness when he dwells in water?” First, you are doing what pleases God.
And second, when you are born from above to God through water, you annul your first birth, which came from desire. In this way you can inherit life; otherwise you cannot.

For the true Prophet swore to us in this way, saying, “Truly, truly, I tell you: unless you are born from water in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Therefore approach in this way. For there is the one who, from the beginning, hovered mercifully over the waters, and who makes herself known to those baptized with the glorious threefold invocation and delivers them from the torment
that is to come, and presents their good deeds after this baptism as an offering to God. There is no longer any refuge [?] these waters, for these alone can extinguish the force of the fire.

But anyone who is unwilling to approach them still has the spirit of wantonness dwelling within him. For this reason he cannot approach the life-giving waters for his own benefit. Approach, then, whether you are righteous or wicked.

For if you are righteous, baptism alone is what you lack for your life. But if you are wicked, this is required: after baptism for the forgiveness of the sins you committed unknowingly, you must repay your wickedness with corresponding good deeds. Therefore, whether you are wicked

or righteous, hurry to be born to God, and do not delay, because delay involves danger, since the appointed time of death is unknown. Therefore, through good deeds, show the likeness of your Father, who gave birth to you through water,
as a lover of truth. Love God, who loves truth; honor him as your Father. This is how to honor him: just as he is righteous, he desires that you too should live righteously.

His righteous will is that no one should act wickedly. Wickedness is murder, adultery, lust, hatred, and anything resembling these. These have many forms. But something must also be combined with them,

which is not found among people, but belongs entirely to the fear of God. I mean that a person should first of all be pure and should not have intercourse with a woman for money, because God's law also commands this. But even if this had not been ordained
by God—that a person should be pure—would you have enjoyed wallowing in mud like filthy pigs? And for this reason, as human beings who have something more within you than speechless animals,
nurture your heart with heavenly thought, and wash your body in baptism. Indeed, bodily purity is truly good, though it is not superior to purity of mind,
but it too is required for goodness. For our Teacher himself addressed some of our people who were Pharisees and scribes—as people set apart
because of their virtues, and as scribes who knew the law better than others. He rebuked them in this way as hypocrites,
because they purified only what was visible to people, but left their souls, which were visible to God alone, in filth.
He therefore rightly used this plain expression, not toward all of them, but toward the hypocrites. For he even commanded people to listen to some of them,
because they had been entrusted with Moses' seat. But to the hypocrites he spoke in this way: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees!”

You hypocrites, you clean the outside of the cup and the bowl, but inside they are full of filth. Blind Pharisees, first clean the inside of the cup and the bowl, so that their outside may also be clean.

Truly, when the mind is enlightened by knowledge, the person who has been enlightened can become good, for purity arising from the inner mind accompanies goodness. There is also proper care for the body.
For care for the mind cannot come from the body, which has no understanding. Thus someone who is clean within can also cleanse his outside. But someone who cleanses only his outside—

does this for praise from people, so that he may be seen, and has nothing before God. Now who does not see that it is good for a man not to have intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period, but only when she is clean?
But you should also have approached intercourse itself for the purpose of having children. If you are unwilling to do this, remember how eagerly you used to pursue purity
when you served idols that have no understanding. Be ashamed that in this case, where it was required—not merely greatly, but more than greatly—
you are unwilling to undertake purity. Consider, then, who it was that urged you on there, and reflect on who it is that now stirs up in you an unwillingness to be pure.
Perhaps one of you will say, “Must I then do everything that we used to practice in connection with idols?” I say, “No, but whatever you did well there,
do here to an even greater degree.” For anything good found in error is taken from the truth, just as, whenever something is practiced wickedly in connection with the truth, it comes from error.
Therefore, seek what is yours on every side, and not what is not yours. Do not say, “We must not do any of the things done by those
who are in error.” For by this reasoning, if an idol worshiper does not murder, we are obliged to murder because the person who is in error did not murder!

But it is not so. Rather, we must do more: if those who remain in error do not murder, we must not even become angry. If someone who is in error does not commit adultery, we must not even lust in the first place.

If someone who is in error loves the person who loves him, we must also love those who hate us. If he lends to those who have resources, we must also lend to those who have none. Page 145. In a word, we are required,
as people who expect to inherit the world that has no end, to do more good than is done by those who are aware only of this world.
For if their good deeds are compared with ours on the day of judgment and are found equal, we will be ashamed of ourselves.
As for them, even their good deeds bring harm upon them as they perish. But when I said that we would be ashamed, I said it because we have not done more than they have,
although we have also known more than they have. But if we are ashamed when we display good deeds equal to theirs, because we have not displayed more than they have,

how much more if we fall short of their good deeds! The true Prophet himself taught that the actions of those who know the truth are indeed compared with the good deeds of those who are in error, when he said to some of those who neglected to come and hear his word:
“The queen of the South will rise with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and look, someone greater than Solomon is here,
and you do not believe.” And to those of the world who were unwilling to repent at his preaching, he spoke as follows:
“The men of Nineveh will rise with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, and look, someone greater than Jonah is here,

and no one believes.” In the same way, against all their leaders he cited people from the nations to condemn those who lived in the fear of God but had not done good deeds even comparable to those of people in error. And likewise,

he taught those who had understanding not merely to do good as the nations did, but to do more than they did. For our discussion arose from the occasion that presented itself: that a man should keep away from a woman during her menstrual period,
and that a man should exercise restraint in intercourse, and should not fail to learn from this purity, even if it is found among those who are in error.

49. The good deeds done by those who are in error serve to condemn those who know God, although those who do them do not gain life through them. For their purity is for the sake of error, not out of fear of the true God, who is the Father of all.
When he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly and, as usual, took food with his dear companions. Afterward he rested. This was what he always did, bringing everyone to the law of God.
He compared the things people believed with what they supposed to be astrological destiny, and showed that the world is not governed by its own will, but by God's grace.
When three months had passed for him, he instructed me to fast for some days. Then he led us out and baptized us in the water of the springs beside the sea. And likewise
the brothers rejoiced with us over my birth through God's gift. A few days later, he was sternly instructing the elders before the whole church.

He said, “Our Lord, who sent us and who was a prophet, told us that the evil one contended against him for forty days. When he could not overcome him, he promised to send messengers from among those who obey him, in order to lead people astray.

Therefore, above all, remember not to receive anyone as an apostle, teacher, or prophet who has not first submitted his preaching for comparison to James, who was appointed, the brother of our Lord, and was entrusted in Jerusalem
with leading the church of the Hebrews. He must come to you with witnesses from there, lest the evil power that contended with our Lord for forty days and achieved nothing,
and finally fell like lightning from heaven to earth, send some preacher to harm you, just as it has now incited Simon to teach error under the pretext of truth.

At another time, too, it may send an apostle, teacher, or prophet to preach in our Lord's name while mixing error into his words. For this reason our Lord himself also said, ‘Many will come to you in sheep's clothing, while inwardly they are ravenous wolves.

You will recognize them by their fruits.’” When he had said these things, he sent those who traveled ahead of him to Antioch in Syria, saying that he intended to remain there for the next three months. When they had set out,
and a large crowd was now pleading with him, Peter healed those who were afflicted by demons and illnesses. He baptized people in the springs beside the sea.
After breaking the Eucharistic bread, he appointed Maron, their host, who was now fully prepared, as bishop. He appointed twelve elders, designated deacons, and enrolled widows.
Then he spoke for the benefit of the whole church, explaining that they should obey their bishop Maron. When his three months had now come to an end,
he took leave of those who were in Tripoli in Phoenicia and traveled on the road to Antioch in Syria.
From Tripoli in Phoenicia.

After we had left Tripoli, we came that same day to Orthosia and stayed there for one day. Then we came to Antaradus. Since many people were with us, Peter said to Nicetas and Aquila, “Because large crowds of brothers are accompanying us,
and considerable jealousy is stirred up against us when we enter a city, I have decided to devise a way by which they will neither be delayed nor prevented from being with us,

and we ourselves will not fall under malicious envy when many people are watching us. I therefore want you, Nicetas and Aquila, to go ahead of us for two reasons: so that we may enter the city of the Gentiles separately.
I know that you are distressed because you are about to move away from us for a stretch [?]
of not even two full days. Believe me, I love you far more than you love me. This is because it was through my hands that you were brought to God. Since, therefore, we love one another,
we do not wish to act beyond what is right, but to concern ourselves, as far as we can [?], with what is beneficial.

I say again that you will not be deprived of my words for even a single day. For, as you yourselves know, I am appointed to remain for three months in these well-known cities. But now, in this nearby Laodicea, go ahead of them.”
“Wait for us in front of its gates, you by yourselves—I say this because of the crowd. Soon, for my part,

I will go ahead of you, and so we will enter quietly and lodge together. I want you to do this in every city, so that we may also escape envy, and so that, through your care, the brothers may find you without distraction at the

lodging place.” When Peter said this, they reluctantly submitted, saying, “This does not trouble us very much, since you are the one giving us instructions: first, because you do and advise everything wisely and well,

having likewise been chosen by the grace of Christ; and second, because we are leaving your side for only one day or two—though even these are many when we do not see our master Peter. Therefore, whatever seems to you
to be helpful, we are ready to do.” When they had said this, they went ahead, having received instructions to tell the people with us not to enter the city all together in a crowd. Then,
when they had gone, I, Clement, was very glad that he wanted me alone to accompany him. I said to him, “I give thanks to God that you did not send me away as you did my companions.
For I might have wasted away from grief.” He said to me, “Then if circumstances should ever require you to be sent away for the sake of teaching, will you die of sorrow?
Did you not consider that you must steadfastly endure whatever happens out of necessity?

Or do you not understand that friends are always present with their friends through their remembrance of them, even when they are physically far away, just as some people, though nearby, are regarded as distant by their companions?”

I said, “My master, do not suppose that I have loved you so much through some [?] impulse or without discernment. Rather, it is because you take the place of everyone for me—the place of father, mother, and brothers.
And after [?], you have become for me the means of reaching the truth that gives me life. For this reason I want to be with you always.
I am also afraid of the desires of my youth, lest, when I leave your side, I become someone different from who I am. For although I am very confident that, even if I leave your side,
I will not fall through desire, it is nevertheless much better and safer for me to be with you continually, because shame before you checks me beforehand. I remember that you said in Caesarea,

‘Anyone who wishes to accompany me rightly may accompany me.’ By ‘rightly,’ I think you meant a man from among his own people, or a sensible woman. For this reason I am suited in every way to accompany you.
And if you wished to do me a great kindness, you would instruct me to serve you in the place of a servant.”
Peter laughed at this and said, “What are you thinking, Clement? Indeed, there is no need for you to fill the place of servants for me! Otherwise, who would look after these fine clothes and rings?
And who, again, would prepare delicious dishes and exquisite meals for me, which require many skilled workers because of their variety,
and all the other things provided, through exploitation, for people agitated by greed, as though for great beasts? But this thought
has entered your mind because you do not understand our way of life: we make do with bread and olives alone, and sometimes vegetables.
Moreover, we have no other tunic or cloak besides what I am wearing, and I need nothing else. For my mind soars, looking toward eternal things, and pays no attention to anything here.

But I have accepted your good intention, and I marvel at how you, a man accustomed to a luxurious life, have so quickly changed your way of life to suit our concerns. For from our childhood, my brother Andrew and I
not only were not brought up in wealth, but poverty even drove us to manual labor. For this reason we now endure hardship easily. So if you would listen to me,
you would allow a working man to fill the place of a servant for you.” When I heard this, I was deeply distressed.
My tears [?], and I marveled at the spirit in which this man spoke, a man worth more than the whole world. When he saw me weeping, he asked why.
I said to him, “What have I done wrong, that you should say this to me?” Peter answered me, “You were the first to do wrong, when you asked this of me.”
to serve me. But I said, “This is not fitting. It is very proper for me to do this for you, but for you, God’s herald and the one who gives life to our souls, this is not appropriate.”
Peter said, “I might have listened to you, had not our Lord himself come to give life to the whole world, although he was free from everyone.”

“What, then?” he said. “He who alone is free endured slavery to teach us not to be ashamed to perform the duties of slaves.” And I said, “I am not so foolish as to suppose that I can defeat you in an argument.”
“But I thank God’s grace for this: that I have found you to take the place of my own people.” He said to me, “Do you really have no one

related to you by birth?” I said, “I have many relatives who are distinguished and closely associated with Caesar. Indeed, for this reason Caesar himself, treating my father as his foster son, sought out for him a wife of noble
birth. By her he had two sons older than me. They were twins and [?] resembled one another, as my father himself used to tell me.

“For I do not remember them, since I was still a small child then. My mother’s name was Metrodora, and my father’s was Faustinus. Of my brothers, one was named Faustinus and the other Faustus, while I
was born last, after them. When I was five years old, my mother had a dream. My father used to say that it warned her that unless she left Rome, taking her two sons with her, within

ten years she would perish with them in a terrible death. My father, therefore, because he loved them very much, provided them with male and female servants, put them aboard a ship, and sent them to Athens so that they could be educated together. But me

alone, aboard a ship, and he sent them to Athens so that they could be educated together. But he kept me alone as his son for consolation, acknowledging that the dream had not ordered me alone to leave Rome

with my mother. When a year had passed, my father sent them money for their expenses, also to find out how they were. But those who were sent did not return. In the third year, my father, again in his anxiety,

sent others with provisions. These returned in the fourth year, saying that not even [?] he had sent provisions. These returned in the fourth year, saying that they had found neither my mother nor my brothers.

“They said that they had never even entered Athens in the first place, and consequently they could not find any trace of them. When my father heard this, he was bewildered by his great sorrow and did not know where to look for them.

“He took me along and went down to the harbor. He questioned many shipowners, asking whether anyone had heard of or seen ships that had been lost during those four years. And while he was speaking to one,

he would turn to another with a different question: whether anyone had seen the bodies of a woman and her two sons washed ashore from the sea. Although they told us many things, they told us nothing certain.
“Because of the uncertainty arising from these many reports, he then left me in Rome, when I was ten years old. And so, weeping, he went out to search for them. From then until now
I have been unable to learn anything about him. But I suppose that he too has died [?], either overcome by grief or through the passage of time.
“The twenty years that have passed suggest to me that this may have happened.” When Peter heard all this, he wept from deep sorrow.
He said to those with him, “If what happened to this man’s father had happened to someone who feared God, he would have regarded his intention to fear God as the cause of his misfortune.
“These things happen to the wretched Gentiles, and we do not know [?]. I called them wretched because, even while they pay the penalty here through misfortunes,

they are deprived of the hope of the world to come and are tormented forever. For those who endure suffering while fearing God suffer as repayment for the wrongs they have committed.” When Peter had said this,
one of us, on behalf of us all, ventured to persuade him that we should first go by sea to the island of Aradus, which was not quite six stadia away, ostensibly to see those two pillars
of vinewood that were there, which were very thick. When Peter heard this, he gave us permission, saying, “When you leave the ship, do not all go together as a group to see them,
so that many people will not turn their attention to you.” We sailed and immediately found ourselves on that island.
When we came out from the god, we went into the place where these pillars stood. Some of us were looking at something else in the surroundings of Piraeus.
Peter, however, was sitting alone on dry ground beside the sea. He saw a woman sitting there and begging, apparently for [?] food. He said to her, “Woman, what limb are you missing,
that you have submitted yourself to all this humiliation? I mean begging. Why have you not worked with the hands God gave you
and earned your daily food by doing so?” She sighed and answered him, “If only I had hands that could serve me!
But now they have only the appearance of hands. They are dead, mutilated by my own bites.” Peter said to her,

“What is the reason you have done this to yourself?” She said, “The reason for this is misery, and nothing else. If I had remained of sound mind, there was a cliff or a deep place from which I could have thrown myself
and escaped my troubles.” Peter said, “Why, woman, do you think that all those who kill themselves escape torment?
Or perhaps their souls die in that terrible torment, while those who kill them here are punished in Sheol?” She answered him, “If only I were convinced that souls really do exist in Sheol!
I would choose to disregard even that torment, thinking that in this way I could embrace my loved ones.” Peter said to her, “Who is it whose loss grieves you so?
I would like to know, woman. If you tell me, in return for this kindness I will convince you that souls live in Sheol.
And instead of a cliff or the depths of the sea, I will give you a remedy by which you may leave this world without torment.” The woman, persuaded by his promise, began to speak as follows:
“As for my family and my homeland, I do not think anyone can persuade me to speak about them. But this much you may readily learn:
only the reason why, in my grief, I disabled my hands by biting them. I am a woman of noble family, and at the ruler’s command
I was married to a man of his family. After having twin sons, I also had another son. After this, my husband’s brother desired me, although I very much wished to live chastely.
Since I could not bring myself to yield to the man who desired me, and did not want to reveal his brother’s desire to my husband, I devised a way neither to defile myself
nor to dishonor my husband’s bed, nor, again, to make his brother hateful in his eyes and bring our whole family into disgrace.
I was compelled to leave the city with my two twin sons until that impure desire subsided. I left my other son with his father. To provide a pretext for these arrangements,
I decided to say that I had seen a dream, in which someone stood over me at night and said to me,

‘Woman, leave here quickly with your two twin sons, until I meet you again to bring you back. Otherwise, you will suffer calamities along with your husband and your children.’ When I told my husband the dream, he became afraid, and with my two

twin sons he provided me with male and female slaves and sent me to Athens, so that his sons might be educated there together. He said, ‘Until the one who appeared to you is pleased for you to return to me.’ But while I, miserable woman, was sailing with my sons,

a violent wind wrecked the ship, and I was thrown ashore at this place during the night. Everyone with us died, but I, weak as I was, was swept along by the surging waves, washed up beside a rock, and sat there.
Hoping to find my sons, I did not throw myself into the depths of the sea, though I could easily have done so then, when my soul was distraught with fear
and I was wretched from my sufferings. By then it was already early morning. I was wailing loudly and crying out bitterly, looking this way and that as I searched for my sons’ dead bodies.

Those who found me clothed me and helped me search for my sons. When they could not find them, they began to comfort me. Some of the women who had gathered there told me, one by one, about their own misfortunes.
I might find comfort in misfortunes like my own. But I was only distressed all the more, for I was not one of those hateful women who find comfort in other people's troubles.
Many of them offered to take me to their homes, but one poor woman from that place pressed me to come and brought me into her house.
She said, “Take heart, woman! My husband too was a sailor, and he died at sea while he was still young. From that time on, I chose to remain a widow out of love for him. So let us share

whatever we can gather with our hands.” But, not to weary you with a long account, I lived with her because she loved her husband. After a little while, my hands—wretched woman that I am—became paralyzed from the bites, while the woman who had taken me in became paralyzed all over.
Now she lies in the house. But the compassion of those women from that time has come to an end. I and the woman in the house have been suffering here, as you see, for a very long time.
I sit begging, so that from what I collect I can also bring food to that wretched companion of mine. Now enough has been said about my affairs. You, then, fulfill what you promised.

Give me the poison, so that I can give some to her too, and she may die.” When the woman said this, Peter was astonished at her and filled with many thoughts. But I, Clement, came up and said to him, “I have been going about looking for you for a long time.
What are we doing now?” Peter told me to go ahead and wait for him in the boat.
I did as I was told. Peter stayed a little longer, as he himself later related everything to me, and his heart was leaping.
He said, “Tell me, woman, your family background and your children's names, and I will give you the poison at once.” But although she was being pressed, she did not want to tell him.
Yet she was eager to receive the poison, so she devised a way to tell him one thing in place of another. She therefore said about herself [?] that she was from Assos,
and that her husband was from Sicily. She also changed the names of her three sons. Peter, thinking that she had told the truth, said to her, “I had hoped, woman, that I would have great joy,
because I had taken you to be a woman whose life I had heard about long ago and know very well.” But she implored him and pleaded with him, saying,
“Tell me, so that I may see whether there is any woman worse off than I am.” Peter, because he did not know how to lie, and also because he truly pitied her, began to speak.
“There is a young man with me who accompanies me out of love for the word of God. He is from the city of Rome. He told me that he had a father, two brothers who were twins,
and a mother, but now he sees none of them. For his mother, as his father related, had seen a dream that she should leave Rome with her two twin sons. Since she left,
she has been nowhere to be found. Her husband too, who is his father, went out to search for them and was not found.” When Peter said this, she lost consciousness from sheer astonishment.
Peter urged her to come to herself and begged her to tell him what had happened to her.
Then the rest of her limbs also went limp, as though from too much wine. But she recovered and washed her face. “The young man you spoke of, Peter,” she said, “is my son!”
Peter, having understood a little, said to her, “First tell me who you are. Otherwise, you cannot see him.”
In her eagerness, she said, “I am that young man's mother!” Peter said to her, “What is his name?”
She said, “Clement.” Peter said, “He is the one who was speaking with me a little while ago, whom I told to go ahead of me to the boat.” She fell down and begged Peter to hurry to the boat.
But he said to her, “If you keep my conditions, I will do what I promised.” She promised to observe everything
that Peter would command her. He said to her, “When you see him, control yourself until we leave the island.”
She said that she would do so. He took her by the hand and led her toward the boat. But when I, Clement, saw that he was bringing the woman,
I smiled and approached, intending to honor her and lead her away. But as soon as I reached for her hand, she cried out loudly and embraced me.
She kept kissing me, but because I did not know her whole story, I pushed her away from me as though she were mad. I was especially upset because I felt ashamed before Peter.
But Peter said to me, “Be still! What have you done, my son Clement, pushing your mother away like this?” When I heard this, I wept and threw myself upon her as she lay there, kissing her.
As soon as this was said to me, I began dimly to recognize her appearance. A great crowd came running to see the woman who had been begging.
They were saying, “Her son, a distinguished man, has recognized her.” When we were about to leave the island immediately, together with my mother, my mother said,
“My dear son, would it be right for me to abandon the woman who took me in? She is poor and lies at home completely paralyzed.”

When Peter heard this, he was amazed, as were all those standing there, at the woman’s good and noble disposition. Peter immediately ordered some people to go and bring that woman. She was brought on a bed and placed before him.

While everyone there listened, Peter said, “If I truly am God’s herald, then, to bring these people to faith, so that they may know that there is one God who made the world, let this woman be healed immediately.”
When he said this, the woman immediately stood up, healed, and fell at Peter’s feet. She kissed her dear companion and asked her
what had happened. She briefly told her the whole story. When the crowd heard it, they were astonished. Peter spoke about God and his way,
and finally added, “Anyone who truly wishes to learn should come to Antioch, for I will be there for three months.
For is it not the case that you can leave your own countries for trade or military service and travel a great distance, but for eternal life
you are unwilling to make even a three-day journey?” After Peter’s address, I gave the woman who had taken my mother in a thousand staters for her needs.

I entrusted her to a good man who was one of the city’s leaders. I also thanked those who had at times encouraged my mother. Then I left the island with Peter and the others, taking my mother with me.
When we came to the place where we were staying, my mother asked me where my father was. I said, “He went out to look for you,
and has never been found again.” When she heard this, she merely sighed, for the great relief and joy she had experienced comforted her.

The next day she sat with another woman and traveled with us in this way. From there we came to Balanea and stayed there for three days. On the following day we came to Gabala, and on the day after that we reached Laodicea.
There Nicetas and Aquila met us outside the gates. After greeting us with kisses, they led us to the house of Marshai. When Peter saw that the city was large and beautiful,
he said, “It is worth staying here for ten days or more.” Nicetas and Aquila asked about the woman and who she was.
