I said, “She is my mother, whom God willed that I should recognize through my lord Peter.” After I said this, he began telling them everything, one detail at a time: how we had entered Aradus and how he had found her begging beside the harbor.
When he asked why she was begging, he learned from her about her family and her whole life, and how she had fallen into such misery. From this came the recognition.
But before he had finished saying these things, while Peter was recounting each detail of how she had been shipwrecked, and before he had even mentioned the names of her two twin sons,
Nicetas and Aquila were astonished and suddenly became agitated. They said, “Are we really hearing this, or is it a dream?”
Peter said, “If we keep quiet, these things are indeed true.” They were silent for a moment, wiping their faces.
Nicetas spoke first and said, “We ourselves are Faustus [?] and Faustinus, the ones you mentioned. For from the very beginning, when you started telling this story, we thought that it concerned us
“What you have been saying is plausible. But because we have been considering how many similar things happen in the world, we have remained silent, watching to see how the matter would turn out.
Then we will reveal who we are.” When Nicetas had said this, both of them went in to their mother weeping. They found her asleep and wanted to embrace her.
But Peter stopped them and said, “Let me bring you to your mother quietly, so that overwhelming, sudden joy does not drive her out of her senses,
especially since she is asleep and her awareness is dulled by sleep.” When our mother awoke from her sleep, Peter said to her, “Woman, I want you to know
that, according to the practices of our religion, we worship one God, who cannot be seen.
This visible world itself belongs to him. We obey him alone, for before everything else he commanded that a person should worship him alone, praise his name, honor other people, be chaste,

and live justly. Moreover, we do not share the tables of the Gentiles unless they have begun to practice righteousness and we have baptized them in the name of the Trinity, which is blessed. Then we share bread with them.
Otherwise, even if someone is a person's father, mother, brother, wife, or son, we cannot share a meal with that person.
Since this is the law of our religion, do not think we are insulting you because you cannot share bread with your son until you share his beliefs.”
When she heard this, she said, “What prevents me from being baptized today? Even before I saw you, I was mocking those who are called gods.

For although I offered them many sacrifices, they did nothing to help me. As for adultery, what could anyone say against me? Not even a purple robe ever enticed me to commit it. Neither poverty nor wealth compelled me.”
While my mother was saying this, my brothers could no longer contain themselves. Nicetas and Aquila stood up and embraced her, weeping bitterly.
She said, “What is this?” Peter said, “Woman, steady your mind so that you can enjoy your sons in good health. These are your sons Faustinus and Faustus, whom you said had died at sea.
How they are still alive, and how one is now named Nicetas and the other Aquila, they themselves will now tell us.” When Peter said this,
my mother fainted from overwhelming joy, and we could scarcely revive her. When she came to herself, she sat down and said,
“My dear sons, I beg you, tell me what happened to you after that bitter night.” Nicetas began to speak: “On that very night, Mother,
when the ship broke apart, some pirates pulled us out, put us aboard a ship, and brought us to Caesarea Stratonis. There they tormented us with hunger
and threatened us with beatings so that we would reveal nothing about them. They also changed our names and then sold us. A distinguished Jewish woman
named Justa bought us, and she and her husband treated us as their sons. She gave us a complete Greek education. When we had grown older,
we came to love this religion. We also loved studying Greek learning, so that when we were among the other Gentiles,
disputing with them, we could expose their error. We also quietly examined the futile arguments of the philosophers, especially the doctrines of the impious—I mean Epicurus and Pyrrho—
so that we would be able to refute them. We approached another man, a companion of my lord Peter named Zacchaeus, and he taught us. When Peter came, we approached him to learn the truth.
We had been like pupils to a certain Simon, and under the pretext of friendship he put us in danger of going astray. There is also another report about a man who appeared

in the kingdom [?], and the assemblies of those who feared God there, that he would live without death and without sorrow [?]. But these things, Mother, we will recount to you at leisure another time. Concerning Simon,

we approached a companion of my lord Peter named Zacchaeus, and he taught us not to be led astray by that magician. When Peter himself came, we approached him so that he would strengthen us and give us assurance about the things belonging to the worship of God.”

For this reason, Mother, we pray that you too may be worthy to receive these good things of which we have been deemed worthy, so that we may share together in one world and at one table. This, then, Mother, is the reason
why you thought we were dying on that bitter night, when we were rescued from the sea after the shipwreck, and you thought you had lost me forever.
When Faustinus said this, our mother fell down and begged and pleaded with Peter to send for her hostess from her home, bring her, and baptize her together with herself,
saying, “So that not even one day may pass, from the day I recovered my sons, without my sharing bread with them.” We too made these same requests, just as our mother did.

Peter said, “What do you think? Am I alone without compassion, that I would not [?] baptize your mother today so that you could share bread with her? But she is required to fast at least one day before baptism.
And this is because a certain remark she made about herself [?] revealed her faith to me.
Otherwise, she would have needed many days to purify herself from paganism.” Clement said to us, “Recall what she said that revealed her faith.”
Peter said, “It was her request that her hostess should also live with her, because she had shown her kindness. She would not have asked this for the woman she loved
unless she had first grasped the great importance of receiving baptism. For this reason I look down on many people who are baptized and say they believe, but do nothing worthy of baptism.
They do not even persuade those they love—I mean their wives [?], their children, or their friends—to come to it. For if they believed that God gives eternal life
to those who are baptized and do good works, they would earnestly urge those they love to be baptized. But perhaps one of you will say, ‘They do love them, yet they are not concerned
about them.’ But this is contempt. For when they see them sick, being led to death, or suffering other misfortunes, they mourn and have compassion on them. Likewise,
if they believed that eternal fire awaits those who do not fear God, they would not stop teaching them. Or, if they saw them resisting, they would mourn over them as over people
who do not believe, like people who are convinced of their torment. And now I will send for her hostess and instruct her. If she accepts our rule, we will then do what is proper in due order.
But since your mother has faithfully set her mind on baptism, let her fast one day.” She swore that during the past two days, because she had been telling that woman about the recognition,
she had been unable to take any food because of her great joy [?], except for a little water yesterday

alone. Peter’s wife supported the woman’s oath, saying, “She has truly spoken no lie.” Aquila, who was now called Faustinus, said, “Then nothing prevents her from being baptized.” But Peter laughed and said, “This was not

a baptismal fast, since it was not undertaken for that purpose.” Faustinus answered, “Then if God wishes our mother not to be separated from our table for even one day from the day she knew and recognized us, he himself arranged beforehand for her to fast.
For just as she preserved her chastity and unknowingly did what accords with the truth, so now too God wished it and arranged beforehand for her to fast.

For just as she preserved her chastity and unknowingly did what accords with the truth, so now too God wished it and arranged beforehand for her to fast one day in advance, without knowing it, for the baptism of truth,
to share in it.” Peter said, “Do not win unfairly by using the argument he has found in God’s providence

and in your mother’s love. Instead, let us do this: you and I together will remain like this today, and tomorrow she will be baptized. For the present hour is not suitable for baptism either.” Thus we all agreed together that this should be our decision.

That evening we took delight in Peter’s teaching, as he showed us from our mother’s experience why acts of chastity are good, while acts of adultery, because they are evil, have a natural power to destroy the whole human race,
even if not quickly, yet eventually. But in all this, acts of chastity were pleasing to God.
For God gives even those who are in error about him a little favor in this world. For that life there is granted only to those who are baptized in hope of him and perform good deeds in chastity.

As you have seen from what happened to your mother—I mean the good things that happened in the end. Perhaps, if she had committed adultery, she would have been killed. But because she remained chaste, God in his mercy turned her murderer away from her.

And he restored to her the children who had been taken from her. But perhaps someone will say, “How many people have perished because of chastity!” I say, however, that this happens through lack of judgment.
For a woman who has understanding is required [?] to flee from association with anyone who desires her impurely, as from a blazing fire and as from a rabid dog, just as your mother

did, because she loved the true beauty of chastity. For this reason she was preserved, and together with you she received knowledge of the kingdom forever. That woman wanted to live in chastity; behold, mercy upon her [?]
Because she was envied by evils full of desire, her enemies were many. But she remained pure in one steadfast commitment to chastity, gained victory over them all, and life is reserved for her.
For even if someone performs every good deed, he is punished for a single sin of adultery, as the prophet said. A chaste woman does God's will and becomes a good reminder of his original creation.
For just as God is one, he created one woman for one man. Moreover, she remains all the more steadfast in chastity if she does not forget her creation, and if she looks ahead to punishment
and recognizes the loss of everlasting good. A chaste woman rejoices in those who wish to live. Righteous women belong to those who fear God.
For a woman who desires chastity is a rule of good conduct. She will quiet occasions for insults by giving no occasion for them. She is insulted as though by an enemy, as
though by an enemy, but she is blessed by God and sought after. A chaste woman pleases God, loves God, gladdens God, and praises God. She gives people no occasion for insult.
A chaste woman delights the church with a good reputation, and her chastity is praised. Moreover, she is also the praise of her teachers and their helper, when they are chaste. A woman
who is chaste adorns herself for the Son of God as for a bridegroom, clothed in the light of chastity. Her beauty is the good conduct of her soul, and her perfumes spread

her good reputation. The beautiful garments she wears are chastity, and the precious pearls she bears are words that teach her chastity. Her appearance, too, when her mind is clear [?]. She looks into a good mirror when she looks toward God. She uses good adornment,
the fear of God, as she instructs her soul. A beautiful woman is not one who is bound in gold, but one who is free from passing desires. A chaste woman is desired by the great King.

She is betrothed to him, preserved for him, and loved by him. A chaste woman gives no occasion for being desired, except by her husband. She loves him with all her heart, kisses him, excites him, and [?], submits to him, and obeys him in everything, except that she must not despise God.

For a woman who obeys God will be chaste in her soul and pure in her body without guards and without [?]. Therefore every man who keeps his wife away from the fear of God is senseless, because if she does not fear God,

she will not fear her husband either. For if she does not fear God, who sees hidden things, how will she be chaste in her hidden thoughts? And how, again, will she become chaste if she does not come to those who teach chastity to hear

their words? How will she receive instruction? And how will she remain chaste without guards if she has no awareness of God's coming judgment and no firm conviction about the loss of everlasting good things that results from a small occasion?

Therefore, in response to this, when she is unwilling to come to words that teach chastity, rebuke her and stir her up. But it is far better if you become her guide and bring her, so that you too will be chaste.

You will want to be chaste if you know the outcome of a chaste marriage, and you will not grow weary. It is not right that you love [?]—I mean being a father—so that you may love children who are your own

and be loved by your children. Anyone who wishes to have a chaste wife must also be chaste himself and pay the debt he owes her. He enjoys himself with her, remains chaste, and pays the debt he owes her. He enjoys himself with her and comes with her to the word that teaches chastity; he does not distress her.
He does not quarrel pointlessly or make himself hateful. He does whatever good deeds he can, and what he cannot accomplish he makes up for with his concern.

A chaste woman does not look for a life of ease. She acknowledges her husband as her master. When he is poor, she endures poverty; if he is hungry, she shares his hunger; when he travels, she accompanies him.

In his distress she encourages him. Even if she has a large dowry, she submits to him as though she had nothing. The husband, for his part, even if his wife is poor, should regard her chastity as a large dowry. A chaste woman, in her eating

and drinking, makes use of what is sufficient for her, lest her body grow strong and crush her soul under the weight of wicked desires. Moreover, she does not associate closely with young men, and she is cautious around old men.

She keeps unruly laughter far from her. Directing her soul toward God alone, she does not go astray. She rejoices when she hears words about chastity, but keeps away from herself words that are not spoken in keeping with chastity.

God is witness that a single act of adultery involves many impulses. This is its evil: although it is worse and more terrible than murder, its terror and wickedness are not visible. For when blood is shed, the body lies dead,
and everyone is appalled at its bitter aftermath. But the sufferings of the soul caused by adultery, although more terrible than these, are not visible to human beings,
and so give greater encouragement to those who act recklessly without fear. Know, human being, whose breath is within you,

so that you may recognize it and not wish to defile it. The breath of God is defiled only by sexual immorality. For this reason it too hastens to hand the one who defiled it over to the fire, delivering its abuser to eternal torment.

While Peter was saying these things to the good and chaste Metrodora, he saw her weeping for joy. He thought she was distressed because of something that had happened to her, and said, “Take courage, woman!
For while many have endured numerous evils because of sexual immorality, you suffered because of chastity. That is why you did not die. But even if you had died, your soul would have been preserved.

You left your lofty homeland for the sake of chastity, but through this circumstance you found the truth and the crown of the kingdom forever. You faced danger in the depths of the sea and did not die.
But even if you had died, that sea, since you would have died for the sake of chastity, would have served as baptism for the life

of your soul. You were separated for a short time from your children, who, because they came from pure seed, proved to be good. Because of your hunger [?], you went about begging for food, and you did not torment your body with sexual immorality, but your soul

you kept alive. You fled from the adulterer so that you would not defile your husband's bed. But God, who saw that your flight was for the sake of chastity, will take the place of a husband. You were alone in distress for a short time, separated from your husband

and your children. Yet you will have to leave them again at the boundary of death. It is far better that you were willingly separated for the sake of chastity than that, unwillingly, after a time, you should have perished with them in their sins.

So let your former afflictions be a great help. For even while they are still upon us, they do not distress us so much because of the hope they produce; indeed, through the hope of good things they even bring joy. But above all, I want you to know

how pleasing chastity is to God. The soul of a chaste woman belongs to God; her choice belongs to God; her will belongs to God; her glory belongs to God. My daughter, chastity is all this good, so that, if the law had not been established

that not even a righteous person may enter the kingdom of God without baptism, perhaps those among the Gentiles who are in error could have lived because of their chastity. For this reason I grieve greatly over those who are chaste while in error, because without a good hope

they have chosen chastity for themselves, yet refuse to come to baptism. For this reason they will not live either, because God has established the rule that anyone who is not baptized shall not enter his kingdom.” When he had said these things, and many more besides, they then went off to sleep.
Discourse Fourteen
Early in the morning, much earlier than usual, Peter awoke, got up, came in to us, woke us, and said to us, “Let Faustus and Faustinus,
and Clement, together with their households, come with me, so that we may go to a secluded place by the sea and find somewhere out of sight where we can baptize her.”

When we were by the sea, he found a clean place among the rocks [?], sheltered from the waves, and baptized her. We brothers withdrew out of consideration for the women and bathed. Then we came and brought the women, and afterward, when we were in a secluded place, we prayed.
Peter sent the women ahead by another road to go to the lodging, apparently because of the crowd.
He instructed that, of the men, only we should accompany our mother and the other women. When we reached the lodging, we waited for him.
We were talking with one another. After many hours, Peter arrived, blessed and broke bread, put salt on it, and handed it first to my mother and afterward to us, her sons.
Then, for the first time, she shared in the bread with [?]. We blessed God. Then Peter, seeing that the people had come in, sat down.
He told us to sit beside him and began speaking, first explaining why he had sent us ahead of him from the baptism and had himself stayed behind and come later. He said that this was the reason:

“After you left the place,” he said, “an old laborer came in, stealthily concealing himself. He had already been spying on us, as he himself finally admitted to me, to see what we were doing when we entered that secluded place.
When I went out, he followed me. At a suitable place he approached me, greeted me, and said to me, ‘You should know that I have been following you for a long time and have wanted to speak with you.
But I held back, afraid that you might be annoyed with me as someone who was not minding his own business. Now, if you wish, I will tell you the things that seem to me to be true.’ I answered, ‘Say
what you think is good, and we will listen to you. Even if what is said is not actually good, you have nevertheless wished, with good intentions, to say things that seemed good to you.’
The old man began speaking as follows: ‘When I saw you bathing in the sea and withdrawing to a secluded place, I approached secretly and watched to see what foolish thing you had gone in to do. But

when I saw that you were praying, I went away. Yet I felt sorry for you again and stayed, so that when you came out I could speak with you and persuade you not to be mistaken. For there is no God, nor anything

that cares for the world. Rather, everything is subject to the stars at birth, as I am convinced by what has happened to me; I have long been persuaded of this teaching. So do not be mistaken, my son. For whether

you pray or not, you happen to receive what has been allotted to you. For if prayers or good deeds were of any help, I would certainly have been living in prosperity. And now, if you are not misled by
these humble clothes I am wearing, you will not dispute what I tell you. I once possessed abundant worldly wealth.
I offered many sacrifices to the gods and gave to the needy. Although I prayed in this way and lived righteously, I could not escape fate.’ I said, ‘What things happened to you?’
He said, ‘I am not concerned to recount my life now. At the end you will hear who I was, what my position was, and to what low estate (low estate) in the world I have come.
For now, I want you to acknowledge that everything is subject to fate.’ I said, ‘If, then, everything is subject to fate, and you are convinced that this is so,
why do you contradict yourself by wanting to give this advice? For if, apart from fate, you cannot even think anything, why do you labor in vain, advising that something should happen

that cannot happen? Furthermore, if the stars at birth do govern things, do not be so eager to persuade me not to fear the one who is also Lord of the stars, by whose will even what could not happen comes to pass.
For anything subject to something else is always compelled to obey it. If, then, a person fears those who are called gods, how much more [?] the stars at birth
are [?]. For even they can do nothing beyond what fate has approved, since they too are subject to universal fate. Universal fate—

they are subject—fate, which is,’ he said, ‘you say, then, [?] is prevented from being subject to anything, and cannot be subjected, being unbegotten and having nothing older than itself.’ While we were saying these things to one another,
a large crowd had gathered around us. Then I looked at the assembly and said, ‘My family and I received from our ancestors the practice of fearing God. And because I held to the commandment

not to hold to the stars at birth—I mean the teaching of Chaldean astrology—for this reason I did not even examine it. And [?] in Chaldean astrology [?] I am not convinced. But the things of which I am convinced, these [?].’
Since you say that the birth horoscope belongs to the art of [?], I cannot refute what you say. But I want to show by another illustration [?] that it is by God's providence that
the world is governed, and that each person receives honor or punishment for what he does. Whether this happens now or then does not concern me.

It is acknowledged, however, that everyone enjoys the results of what he does. But here is a demonstration that astrological destiny does not exist: among us standing here, is there anyone who lacks his sight, whose hand is withered, or whose leg is lame,
or who has some other bodily condition from which he cannot recover or be restored, and which is beyond all physicians? Nor do the Chaldean astrologers promise to heal him,

because such a thing has never happened in the whole history of the world. But by asking God, I would give healing to someone who, according to his birth horoscope, could never recover or be made well. If, then, this should happen in this way,

all sins, wicked deeds, and impurities are brought about by the stars [?], and the stars are appointed by God to do this, to be the agents of every evil, then the sins of every
person attach to him—to the one who wills fate.” The old man answered, “You have truly spoken well. Yet my conscience resists all your remarkable demonstrations.
For I am a Chaldean astrologer, and I formerly lived in Rome. I became friends with a man who belonged to Caesar's family, and I examined his horoscope and his wife's on their behalf.

I investigated carefully and understood everything that could be found in their destinies. Her destiny said this: that she would become an adulteress, fall in love with her slave, and die in water in a foreign country.
And that is just what happened. She desired her slave [?], and because she could not endure the disgrace, she fled with him.

She went to a foreign country, had relations with him there, and then perished in the sea.” I answered him, “But how do you know that the woman who fled had relations with her slave in a foreign country,
and then died after becoming his?” The old man said, “I know for certain. But in fact, it was not that she became his—something I did not even say. Rather, after she went away,
her husband's brother told me everything about her desire, and how he, being a chaste man, and also because he was her husband's brother, did not want to defile her marriage bed.
And how she, that poor woman, because she too feared disgrace, [?]. For no one can be angry with her, because these things came about through fate.” These things,

and the words of the old man, who had spoken of him as dead, [?] that he was your father. But I did not want to tell him about you until I had first revealed these things to you. I learned where he was staying,

and also told him where I was lodging, so that he would know for certain. I asked him only this: “What is the old man's name?” He said, “Faustus.” “And what did he say the names of his twin sons were?”
He replied, “Faustus and Faustinus.” “And what is your third son's name?” He said, “Clement.” “And their mother's?” He said, “Metrodora.” And I [?], out of compassion
on my part, dismissed the gathering and came to you, so that I could reveal this to you after we had shared the bread. But I could not tell you these things before you had received your portion,
lest you be overcome with grief and be mourning on the day of baptism, when even the angels rejoice.” While Peter was saying these things, we all wept with our mother.

When he saw us weeping, he said, “Now let each of you, in reverence toward God, bravely bear what has been said. For your father did not die today, but long ago, just as you yourselves supposed and also said.”
As Peter said these things, our mother could not bear it, and cried out, “Alas for me, my husband! Because you loved us, you died unjustly, while we are alive,

Both of them suddenly fell silent from joy. They wanted to speak to one another, but their tongues were tied by their overwhelming joy.
But after a little while my mother said, “I have received you back, Faustus, who were dearer to me than everything! How can you be alive?
You, whom we heard only recently had died! But now, here are Faustus, Faustinus, and Clement.” When she said this, all three of us threw ourselves upon him, and as
we kissed him, we dimly recalled his appearance. When Peter saw this, he said to him, “Are you Faustus [?], this woman’s husband and the father of her children?” He said, “I am.”
Peter said to him, “Why, then, did you tell me about what happened to you as though it concerned someone else—

about his sufferings, his troubles, and his grave?” Our father answered him, “I belong to Caesar’s family, and because I did not want to become a spectacle, I constructed the story around someone else,

so that my identity would not become known. I was sure that if I were recognized, the rulers in the various regions, when they heard, would try to persuade me in order to please Caesar, and would bring me the good things of the world,
which I had renounced. For while I was deeply mourning my loved ones as people who had died a miserable death, I could not give myself over to the world’s luxury.” And Peter said

to him, “You did these things as you thought best. But when you argued about fate, were you being dishonest, or were you speaking sincerely?” Our father said, “I am not lying to you. In truth, just as
the horoscope stood, so I maintained it. For I was not unacquainted with that discipline.

But a certain distinguished Chaldean astrologer, an Egyptian named Anubion, accompanied me. From the beginning of my travels abroad, he became my friend, and he informed me of the death of my wife and children.”
Peter said, “Then have you now been convinced by what has actually happened that fate is nothing?” Our father answered him, “I must disclose to you everything that comes into my mind,

so that I may hear the answers to these things and be able [?] to learn. That is, I admit that the Chaldean astrologers are wrong about many things, but I also know that they are right about many things.
I therefore suppose that perhaps those who examine things carefully are right, while the errors they make happen through lack of learning. Thus,
as it seems to me, the discipline itself remains sound; that is, they make false statements through ignorance, because not everyone is capable of examining things carefully.”
Peter said, “Consider for me whether the things they get right are [?]. For events in the world happen to agree with them; it is not because they speak on the basis of careful observation.

For it is inevitable that, out of the many things they say, some will happen.” The old man said, “How, then, can we become convinced about this—whether fate exists or not?” While both of them were silent,
I said, “Since I am thoroughly acquainted with this discipline, my lord and father, would I not wish that Anubion himself were nearby, and that a debate about fate could take place before my father?
For the matter could be made clear in this way, if the inquiry took place between an expert and another practitioner of his discipline.” My father answered and said,
“How, then, can someone meet with Anubion?” Peter said, “In Antioch. For I hear that Simon the magician is there,
whom Anubion accompanies, and [?]. So when we go there, if we find them, we shall have this inquiry.”
After we had discussed many things, rejoiced over the reunion that had taken place, and given thanks to God, we went to dinner, since evening was already upon us.
